_comment: THE FRAME WIRE FORMAT, pinned. `BFR1` + rows:u32 + cols:u32 + rows*cols float64, ALL BIG-ENDIAN, C order, then base64. A frame is the payload of a reach, so every language that carries one implements this. Same idiom as contract_vectors.json: the bytes are the contract, and a second implementation is checked against them rather than against a description it has to interpret.
_replaces: base64 of a NumPy .npy buffer (until 2026-08-04). .npy spells its shape as a Python dict literal in ASCII, so a JS or C carrier had to parse Python syntax; a 2x2 frame cost 128 bytes of header for 32 bytes of data. decode_frame still READS .npy so frames already in flight stay readable.
_how_to_verify: base64-decode `encoded`, check the first 4 bytes are 'BFR1', read two big-endian uint32 for shape, read the rest as big-endian float64 in C order, and compare with `values`.

vectors.name: single_cell
vectors.note: the smallest frame; header dominates, which is the point of a 12-byte one

vectors.name: two_by_two
vectors.note: exact binary fractions — any float64 reader reproduces these

vectors.name: negative_and_zero
vectors.note: sign bit and positive zero survive the round trip

vectors.name: wide_row
vectors.note: T=1: one ordered step, five features

vectors.name: tall_column
vectors.note: F=1: three ordered steps, one feature. Distinct from wide_row and the header proves it

vectors.name: fractional
vectors.note: values with no exact binary form — pins the float64 bits, not a decimal rendering
